name: ATTINY1616-MNR
title: ATtiny1614/1616/1617 tinyAVR 1-series 8-bit AVR microcontrollers, 20 MHz, 16 KB Flash, 2 KB SRAM, 256 B EEPROM, 1.8 V to 5.5 V
summary: An 8-bit AVR microcontroller family with a two-cycle hardware multiplier, running at up to 20 MHz from 1.8 V to 5.5 V, with 16 KB of self-programmable Flash, 2 KB SRAM and a 256-byte EEPROM, packaged in 14, 20 or 24 pins. Its peripherals are one TCA, two TCB and one TCD timer, an RTC with periodic interrupt, a USART, SPI, an I2C-compatible TWI up to 1 MHz, two 10-bit 115 ksps ADCs, three 8-bit DACs, three analog comparators, a capacitive touch controller (PTC), two-LUT custom logic, an event system and a CRC memory scan; programming and debug use the one-wire UPDI pin. ATTINY1616-MNR is the 20-pin VQFN (3 x 3 mm) part with 18 I/O lines, rated 20 MHz at 1.8 V to 5.5 V supply and -40 °C to +105 °C, on tape and reel.
key_figures: 8-bit AVR, up to 20 MHz, two-cycle hardware multiplier, two-level interrupt controller
16 KB Flash (64-byte pages), 2 KB SRAM, 256 B EEPROM, plus one user row page
Flash 10,000 cycles, EEPROM 100,000 cycles, retention 40 years at 55 °C
0-5 MHz at 1.8 V to 5.5 V; 0-10 MHz at 2.7 V to 5.5 V; 0-20 MHz at 4.5 V to 5.5 V
16/20 MHz internal RC, 32.768 kHz ULP internal RC, 32.768 kHz crystal, external clock
two 10-bit 115 ksps ADCs, three 8-bit DACs (one to a pin), three comparators, references 0.55/1.1/1.5/2.5/4.3 V
PTC with up to 14 self-capacitance and 49 mutual-capacitance channels
18 general purpose I/O, all with external interrupt
14-pin SOIC150, 20-pin SOIC300, 20-pin VQFN 3x3 mm, 24-pin VQFN 4x4 mm
-40 °C to 105 °C or -40 °C to 125 °C by order code

operation.text: AVR CPU at up to 20 MHz with single-cycle I/O access, a two-level interrupt controller and a hardware multiplier that takes two cycles. 16 KB Flash that the device can program itself, 256 bytes EEPROM, 2 KB SRAM. Flash endures 10,000 write/erase cycles and EEPROM 100,000; data retention is 40 years at 55 °C. Power-on reset and brown-out detector are built in. Clocks: 16/20 MHz internal RC, 32.768 kHz ultra-low-power internal RC, 32.768 kHz crystal oscillator, external clock. Programming and debug go through a single-pin UPDI. Sleep modes: Idle (peripherals running, immediate wake), Standby (selected peripherals running) and Power-Down (data kept).

One 16-bit TCA with three compare channels and its own period register; two 16-bit TCBs with input capture; one 12-bit TCD for control applications; a 16-bit RTC clocked from crystal, external clock or internal RC; a windowed watchdog with its own oscillator; one USART (fractional baud generator, auto-baud, start-of-frame detection); one SPI, master or slave; one TWI with dual address match covering 100 kHz, 400 kHz and 1 MHz I2C modes; three fast analog comparators; two 10-bit 115 ksps ADCs; three 8-bit DACs, one of which reaches a pin; references of 0.55, 1.1, 1.5, 2.5 and 4.3 V; an event system; custom logic with two LUTs; a CRC scan of memory; and a touch controller for buttons, sliders, wheels and 2D surfaces with wake on touch and a driven shield, up to 14 self-capacitance and 49 mutual-capacitance channels. Every general purpose pin can raise an external interrupt. Up to 22 I/O lines. Temperature ranges -40 °C to 105 °C and -40 °C to 125 °C.
Silicon errata and clarifications for these devices are published in document DS80000886.

The ATtiny1614, ATtiny1616 and ATtiny1617 have identical memories (16 KB Flash, 2 KB SRAM, 256 B EEPROM) in 14, 20 and 24 pins. Within the tinyAVR 1-series, a part with more Flash and the same pin count runs the same code unchanged, since it is pin-compatible and has the same or more features; a part with less Flash may need code changes because some peripherals have fewer instances. A part with fewer pins has fewer features. Parts with other Flash sizes generally differ in SRAM and EEPROM too.
On both VQFN packages the large exposed pad under the body is to be soldered to ground for mechanical stability.

16 KB of in-system reprogrammable Flash holds the program. AVR instructions are 16 or 32 bits wide and the program counter is 13 bits. The Flash can be split into boot, application code and application data sections with restricted access between them. It appears in the data space from 0x8000 for LD/ST, and from 0x0000 for LPM. The CRC scanner is a bus master.

The 2 KB SRAM holds data and the stack. The 256-byte EEPROM supports single-byte reads and writes through the NVM controller. The user row (USERROW) is one extra EEPROM page for settings: the CPU reads and writes it like EEPROM, the UPDI can write it even on a locked device, and chip erase leaves it untouched.
A three-byte signature in its own address space identifies the device: 0x1E 0x94 0x21 for the ATtiny1616.

All peripheral registers are in the I/O space. Addresses 0x00 to 0x3F are reachable in one cycle with IN and OUT; 0x0040 to 0x0FFF use LD/LDS/LDD and ST/STS/STD. Registers 0x00 to 0x1F are bit-addressable with SBI and CBI and testable with SBIS and SBIC; SBI and CBI touch only the named bit, so they are safe on flag registers cleared by writing 1. Reserved bits are written as 0 and reserved addresses are never written. Four general purpose I/O registers, GPIOR0 to GPIOR3 at 0x1C to 0x1F, are bit-accessible storage for flags and variables.

Writing any value other than the valid key into FUSE.LOCKBIT locks the device: the UPDI then cannot read Flash (all sections), SRAM, EEPROM or fuses, while the application keeps normal access. Only a chip erase unlocks, and it removes the application data.

Fuses are nonvolatile configuration, valid from power-up. The CPU and the UPDI can read them; only the UPDI can program them. Their values are copied into the target registers at the end of start-up, so a changed fuse takes effect after the next reset. They come pre-programmed and can be changed; reserved bits are written as 1.

Factory data: a three-byte device ID that tells software the device type, memory sizes, pin count and die revision; a ten-byte unique serial number; two temperature sensor calibration bytes (TEMPSENSE0 gain, unsigned; TEMPSENSE1 offset, signed); and four signed bytes giving the OSC20M frequency error measured in production at 16 MHz and 20 MHz, each at 3 V and 5 V.
FUSE.WDTCFG fields WINDOW and PERIOD are copied to WDT.CTRLA at reset, so the watchdog can run from boot.
FUSE.BODCFG sets the BOD level, sample frequency and modes for active and sleep; its bits are copied to BOD.CTRLA and BOD.CTRLB at reset.
FUSE.OSCCFG.FREQSEL picks 16 MHz or 20 MHz for OSC20M and the matching factory calibration loaded into CAL20M and TEMPCAL20M; OSCLOCK locks the OSC20M calibration registers.

APPEND marks where application code stops and BOOTEND where boot stops, each counted in 256-byte blocks. APPEND = 0x00 makes everything from BOOTEND x 256 to the end of Flash application code. BOOTEND = 0x00 makes the whole Flash the boot section, and so do both fuses at 0x00.

Each vector belongs to one peripheral instance, which may have several sources. A source sets its flag in the peripheral's INTFLAGS register and is enabled in its INTCTRL register; a request is raised while flag and enable are both set, and stays until the flag is cleared. Global interrupt enable must also be set.
SYSCFG holds the die revision ID, which the CPU can read to adapt to the part revision.

8-bit AVR RISC core with 135 instructions, a hardware multiplier and 32 8-bit working registers wired to the ALU. Harvard architecture with separate program and data buses and a one-stage pipeline: the next instruction is fetched while one executes, so instructions complete every clock, up to 1 MIPS per MHz. The CPU clock CLK_CPU is not divided internally. Direct addressing covers 64 KB of unified memory; 8-, 16- and 32-bit arithmetic are supported. Configuration change protection guards critical settings.

Register-to-register and register-immediate arithmetic run in one clock with the result written back to the register file, and update the status register. The multiplier forms a 16-bit product from two 8-bit operands in two CPU cycles, for signed or unsigned integers, signed or unsigned fractions, signed by unsigned integers and signed by unsigned fractions.

After reset the CPU starts at Flash address 0x0000. Calls and interrupts push the return address as a word pointer, low byte first at the higher address. The stack lives in SRAM and grows downward; after reset SP points to the top of SRAM. A program that moves the stack must keep it above the SRAM start and set it before any call or interrupt. A write to SPL blocks interrupts until either four instructions have run or another I/O write occurs, whichever is first. SREG is not saved automatically on interrupt entry; the handler saves it if needed.

32 general purpose 8-bit registers in their own address space, all with single-cycle access. The immediate-operand instructions (LDI, CPI, SUBI, SBCI, ANDI, ORI) reach only R16 to R31. R26 to R31 pair into the 16-bit X, Y and Z pointers (low byte at the lower address) with displacement, post-increment and pre-decrement addressing; Z can also point into program memory.

Wide peripheral registers go through a temporary register on the 8-bit bus. Write the low byte first, then the high byte (the low byte is latched and both update together); read the low byte first, which latches the high byte for the next read. A 24-bit register uses two temporary registers, least significant byte first. An interrupt that touches a wide register of the same peripheral can corrupt the sequence, so interrupts are disabled around such accesses, or the handler saves and restores the temporary register.

Protected I/O registers and NVM self-programming are unlocked by writing a signature to CPU.CCP: IOREG for protected registers, SPM for writes to the NVM command register. The protected write or instruction must follow within four instructions; for registers with an enable or lock bit, that bit is written to 1 in the same write. Other I/O or data writes, Flash/NVMCTRL/EEPROM accesses or SLEEP end the window. During the window interrupts, including NMI, are held pending and then served by priority. A write without the unlock leaves the register unchanged.

The core has native debug support reached through UPDI: two hardware breakpoints, breaks on change of flow, on interrupts and by the BREAK instruction, run-time read-out of SP, PC and SREG, and register file read and write while stopped.

NVMCTRL is the CPU's path to the nonvolatile blocks: Flash, EEPROM, fuses, signature row and user row. Flash mainly holds program but can hold data; EEPROM can be programmed while code runs from Flash. It supports self-programming and boot loaders, and three write-protected Flash sections.

Flash is written or erased a whole page at a time. FUSE.BOOTEND and FUSE.APPEND split it in 256-byte blocks into BOOT, APPCODE and APPDATA. Write protection goes one way: BOOT code may write APPCODE and APPDATA, APPCODE code may write APPDATA, and APPDATA code may write neither Flash nor EEPROM. The CPU never writes the BOOT section. NVMCTRL.CTRLB bits APCWP and BOOTLOCK lock further changes to APPCODE and BOOT until the next reset; BOOTLOCK also stops reads and execution from BOOT.
EEPROM is organised in pages but erases and writes with byte granularity: only bytes loaded into its buffer are erased or written.

Flash, EEPROM and user row share one page buffer, so only one is programmed at a time. Writes to the memory addresses fill it; the low address bits choose the location, and each write ANDs into what is there. The buffer is cleared to all ones after a reset, a page write or erase, a Page Buffer Clear command, or a wake-up from sleep. Reading any array during a write or erase stalls the bus until it finishes.

A Flash page must be erased before it is written; writing an unerased page corrupts it. Use Erase and Write Page (ERWP) on a filled buffer, or Erase Page (ER) after writing one byte anywhere in that page, then load the buffer and Write Page (WP). To issue a command: wait until EEBUSY and FBUSY in NVMCTRL.STATUS read 0, write the SPM key to CPU.CCP, then write the command to NVMCTRL.CTRLA.CMD within four instructions. The CPU halts during Flash write and erase and during EEPROM Erase (EEER), but runs during EEPROM write and erase. Page Buffer Clear (PBC) halts the CPU for seven cycles. Chip Erase (CHER) clears Flash and EEPROM to all ones regardless of BOOTLOCK and APCWP, keeping EEPROM if EESAVE is set. Write Fuse (WFU) is available only to the UPDI: load NVMCTRL.ADDR and NVMCTRL.DATA, run the command, and reset for the new value to apply; fuses are read with normal loads.

For a time after power-on reset NVMCTRL refuses NVM writes and FBUSY and EEBUSY read 1; both must read 0 before the buffer is loaded or a command is given. Setting RSTPINCFG to UPDI, or clearing TOUTDIS in FUSE.SYSCFG0, removes this time-out.

At low VDD a write can fail or the CPU can misexecute. Holding the device in reset with the BOD while the supply is too low, using the VLM to avoid starting an EEPROM write near the BOD level, or adding an external low-voltage reset circuit prevents this. A reset during a write aborts the write.

With no write in progress, NVMCTRL sleeps with the system. A write in progress keeps the NVM, its controller and the system clock running until it finishes, in every sleep mode including Power-Down. The EEPROM Ready interrupt wakes the device only from Idle. Waking from sleep clears the buffer of pending page data.

CLKCTRL routes, selects and divides the clocks. Peripherals request the clocks they need and the sources start automatically. Internal sources are OSC20M (16/20 MHz) and OSCULP32K (32.768 kHz ultra low power); external ones are the XOSC32K crystal oscillator and the EXTCLK input. The main clock can be switched safely at run time, and its prescaler has 12 settings from 1x to 64x.

CLK_MAIN feeds the CPU, RAM, Flash and I/O bus and always runs in Active and Idle, and in Standby when requested. It is divided into CLK_CPU (CPU, SRAM and NVM access) and CLK_PER (the other peripherals). Asynchronous clocks: CLK_RTC for RTC/PIT, CLK_WDT for the watchdog, CLK_BOD for the BOD in sampled mode, and CLK_TCD for TCD; each is requested when its peripheral is enabled, and the RTC and TCD sources are changed only with the peripheral disabled. The main clock source is chosen in CLKCTRL.MCLKCTRLA.CLKSEL. TOSC1, TOSC2 and CLKOUT exist only on packages that bond those pins.

An unused source stops. Setting RUNSTDBY in an oscillator's control A register keeps it running in every mode except Power-Down and removes its start-up delay when a peripheral asks for it. In Standby the main clock runs only if requested or held by RUNSTDBY; in Power-Down it stops once NVM operations are done.

Any internal oscillator can drive CLK_MAIN. Hardware blocks unsafe switches: a switch to an external source waits until edges are seen, and until then no other switch is possible without a reset. SOSC in CLKCTRL.MCLKSTATUS shows a switch in progress; EXTS and XOSC32KS show external source stability. If an external main clock fails, only the watchdog can recover the device through a system reset. The prescaler divides CLK_MAIN by 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 6, 10, 24 or 48 to make CLK_PER. MCLKCTRLA and MCLKCTRLB are protected by CCP.

After any reset CLK_MAIN comes from OSC20M divided by 6, at 16 or 20 MHz as FUSE.OSCCFG.FREQSEL selects. Factory calibration is loaded at reset into CAL20M (centre frequency, CLKCTRL.OSC20MCALIBA) and TEMPCAL20M (temperature slope, OSC20MCALIBB); these are CCP-protected and can be locked by the OSCLOCK fuse or, when OSC20M is the main clock, by LOCKEN. It starts in four oscillator cycles after its analog start-up. Changing the calibration can overshoot the frequency, so the main clock is first prescaled to no more than a quarter of the maximum allowed and restored afterwards. For finer accuracy the signature row stores the production frequency error as a signed compressed Q1.10 byte (sign in the top bit, the seven lower bits of the Q1.10 value).

The 32.768 kHz ultra-low-power oscillator trades accuracy against a crystal for very low power. It supplies the 1.024 kHz clock used by RTC, WDT and BOD. Start-up is its oscillator start-up time plus four cycles.

EXTCLK is taken straight from its pin, which becomes the clock input automatically when a peripheral asks for it; it starts in two cycles. XOSC32K runs a 32.768 kHz crystal on TOSC1 and TOSC2, or takes a 32.768 kHz external clock on TOSC1, as the SEL bit in CLKCTRL.XOSC32KCTRLA chooses. It must be enabled with ENABLE before it can run, and then overrides the pin settings. The CSUT bits set the crystal start-up time; with an external clock on TOSC1 start-up is two cycles.

SLPCTRL moves the device between Active and three sleep modes: Idle, Standby and Power-Down. Any sleep mode can be entered from Active. To sleep, enable at least one wake-up interrupt and global interrupts (with none, only a reset wakes the device), select the mode and set the enable bit in SLPCTRL.CTRLA, then execute SLEEP. An interrupt wakes the device, runs its handler and resumes after the SLEEP instruction; any reset ends sleep and restarts from the reset vector. Register file, SRAM and registers keep their contents.

Idle: the CPU stops, every peripheral keeps running and any interrupt wakes the device. Standby: each peripheral runs or stops according to its RUNSTBY bit, so current lies between Idle and Power-Down; the ADC can SleepWalk. Power-Down: only BOD, WDT and the PIT run, and the wake-up sources are pin change, PIT, VLM, TWI address match and CCL.

Wake-up takes six CLK_PER cycles plus the start-up of the main clock source. Idle keeps the source running; Standby may; in Power-Down only OSCULP32K and the RTC clock may run, for the BOD or WDT. Setting FUSE.BODCFG.ACTIVE to 0x3 makes wake-up wait until the BOD is ready, so code never runs on a low supply.
A debugger break wakes the device from sleep into Active, even with no interrupt pending.

RSTCTRL returns the device to its initial state and records the reset cause in RSTCTRL.RSTFR. Supply sources are POR and BOD; user sources are the RESET pin, the watchdog, software reset and UPDI reset. Some sources are enabled by fuses or software. After any reset, registers loaded from fuses or the signature row are refreshed.

The POR detector is always on and holds the device in reset while VDD is below its threshold VPOT; once VDD rises above it (and RESET, if used, is high), reset is released after the time-out tTOUT. RESET may be tied to VDD or held low externally to extend reset.

The BOD compares VDD with a fuse-selected level and resets the device when VDD falls below VBOT-; reset is released tTOUT after VDD returns above VBOT+. When the application does not use the BOD it is still forced to a minimum level during internal reset and chip erase.

operation.topic: Software, external, watchdog and UPDI reset
operation.text: Writing 1 to SWRE in RSTCTRL.SWRR resets at once and holds reset until the sequence completes. The external RESET pin is enabled by FUSE.SYSCFG0.RSTPINCFG; while it is low the device stays in reset. A watchdog not cleared in time resets the device. The UPDI has its own reset source used only by programmers and debuggers.

Reset lasts while any source is active (RESET low, or VDD below the POR or BOD threshold), then an internal initialisation runs. That initialisation is lengthened by the start-up time in FUSE.SYSCFG1.SUT and, if FUSE.SYSCFG0.CRCSRC enables it, by a CRC memory scan. RSTCTRL works in Active and all sleep modes.

CPUINT prioritises interrupt requests, with a separate vector for each source. A non-maskable interrupt serves critical functions; one vector can be raised to level 1 (high); the rest are level 0, served by static priority or optional round robin. Vectors can be placed after the boot section or in the application section (IVSEL), and a compact vector table (CVT) is available. A request waits until it has priority; after a handler returns, one instruction runs before any pending interrupt.

Optionally set IVSEL, CVT and LVL0RR in CPUINT.CTRLA and the level-1 vector in CPUINT.LVL1VEC; enable the interrupt in the peripheral; set the I bit in CPU.SREG. Flags are not cleared automatically when the handler runs. Unused vector locations can hold ordinary code.

On a 16 KB device the fastest response is one cycle to finish the current instruction, two to push the PC and three for the JMP to the handler. A multi-cycle instruction finishes before the interrupt is taken. From sleep the response adds five clock cycles plus the start-up time of the sleep mode. Returning from a handler takes four to five cycles.

An NMI runs regardless of the I bit, never changes it and cannot be interrupted; among NMIs the lowest vector address wins. Which sources are NMIs is fixed by the device, and they must be enabled before use. The level-1 interrupt, chosen by writing its vector number to CPUINT.LVL1VEC, can interrupt level-0 handlers. Among level-0 requests, static scheduling gives the lowest vector the highest priority; writing a vector number Y to CPUINT.LVL0PRI makes Y lowest and Y+1 highest. Round robin (LVL0RR in CPUINT.CTRLA) has hardware update LVL0PRI with the last acknowledged vector so every request is eventually served. RESET and NMI always come first.
With CVT set in CPUINT.CTRLA the table shrinks to three vectors: NMI at vector address 1, the level-1 interrupt at 2, and all level-0 interrupts sharing address 3.
A level-1 handler that is not written correctly can trap the program in a level-1 loop. CPUINT.STATUS shows the current level state, which lets a debugger check that the right RETI ran.

EVSYS carries signals from one peripheral (generator) to others (users) through channels without the CPU, with short, predictable delay. Up to four asynchronous and up to two synchronous channels; each channel takes one generator, but many users may listen to one channel and several channels may use the same generator. Generators and users include the ADCs, comparators, port pins, RTC, timers and CCL; software and the peripheral clock can also generate events. An event is a one-clock pulse or a level.

Each user has its own multiplexer choosing a channel; users that accept asynchronous events also accept synchronous ones. Users of both kinds are set in EVSYS.ASYNCUSERn, synchronous-only users in EVSYS.SYNCUSERn; all default to off. Channel generators are set in EVSYS.ASYNCCHn and EVSYS.SYNCCHn and default to none. Writing 1 to a bit of EVSYS.ASYNCSTROBE or SYNCSTROBE inverts that channel for one system clock, a software event that users treat like any other.

Three channels can be driven out asynchronously on pins EVOUT[2:0]: choose the channel in EVSYS.ASYNCUSER8, ASYNCUSER9 or ASYNCUSER10, optionally configure the pin, and set the EVOUTn bit in PORTMUX.CTRLA.

The peripheral clock serves the registers and software events. Routing works in every sleep mode without a clock; only software events need the clock. EVSYS has no interrupts, no CCP, and is unaffected by debug.
PORTMUX enables or disables pin functions and moves peripherals between their default and alternate pins.

Each PORT instance (PORTA, PORTB, PORTC) has up to eight pins, each with its own direction (DIR) and output (OUT) bit, pull-up, inversion and input sense configuration. The input is synchronised to CLK_PER into PORTx.IN and can be read in input or output mode. Asynchronous pin-change sensing raises interrupts and events and can wake the device from every sleep mode, even with CLK_PER stopped. Dedicated set, clear and toggle registers give hardware read-modify-write, and virtual port registers map DIR, OUT, IN and INTFLAGS into the bit-accessible I/O space.

After reset every output is off (tri-stated) and the digital input buffers are on, even without a clock. Writing 1 to bit n of DIRSET or DIRCLR turns pin n's driver on or off without disturbing other pins; OUTSET, OUTCLR and OUTTGL set, clear and toggle the output, and writing 1 to a PORTx.IN bit toggles OUT too. DIRTGL toggles direction. Turning off the digital input buffer on pins that are unused or carry analog signals gives the lowest current. Debugger pins may be configured otherwise for their special function.

PORTx.PINnCTRL holds INVEN, which inverts input and output for the pin (and toggling it makes an edge seen by peripherals, interrupts and events), PULLUPEN, which enables the pull-up (disconnected while the pin is an output), and ISC, which picks the interrupt sense or INPUT_DISABLE. With INPUT_DISABLE the IN bit stops changing, which saves power and can cut noise on analog pins.

An enabled peripheral connected to a pin (through PORTMUX or its own multiplexer) takes over that pin's behaviour in its own way, and may leave some aspects to PORT. Pins not overridden stay general purpose I/O.

Any pin can be an interrupt source, set in its ISC field; the flag INTn is set in PORTx.INTFLAGS. Toggling INVEN in the same cycle as changing ISC may lose the edge; disabling the input while an interrupt is being synchronised may give that interrupt when re-enabled; changing ISC during synchronisation may lose it. Pins 2 and 6 of each port sense fully asynchronously; the others are partially asynchronous.

Every pin is an asynchronous event generator whose event is the pin level when the input buffer is on and zero when it is off; PORT takes no events. Pin settings do not depend on sleep mode except interrupts and input synchronisation, which use CLK_PER and halt when it stops. All pins can wake the device. In debug halt the PORT keeps running.

The BOD watches VDD and resets the device below a programmable level. Its modes are Enabled (always on), Sampled (switched on briefly at a fixed rate) and Disabled, chosen separately for active and sleep. A voltage level monitor (VLM) with interrupt warns when VDD nears the BOD level; its threshold is set as a percentage above the BOD level. The BOD is set mainly by fuses and must be enabled by the user.

Level and active/Idle mode are loaded from fuses at reset and cannot be changed by software; the Standby/Power-Down mode also starts from fuses but software may rewrite BOD.CTRLA.SLEEP (CCP-protected). Entering Standby or Power-Down switches the BOD to the SLEEP mode, and waking returns it to the ACTIVE mode. VLMIE in BOD.INTCTRL enables the VLM, VLMCFG picks a crossing from above, below or either way, and VLMLVL in BOD.VLMCTRLA sets the threshold. The VLM follows the BOD mode: off when the BOD is off, sampled when it is sampled. The VLM interrupt does not run while the CPU is halted in debug.

VREF supplies one reference to each ADC and one shared by each AC and DAC pair, each selectable as 0.55, 1.1, 1.5, 2.5 or 4.3 V from a bandgap through a buffer. ADCnREFSEL and DACnREFSEL in VREF.CTRLx choose the levels; the default is 0.55 V. A reference turns on when its peripheral asks for it; the force-enable bits ADCnREFEN and DACnREFEN in VREF.CTRLB keep it on to shorten start-up, at the cost of current.

The WDT resets the system if software does not execute WDR within the time-out, which recovers from runaway or deadlocked code. It runs from the 1.024 kHz output of OSCULP32K, independent of the system clock, so it still resets the device if the main clock fails, and it runs in Active and all sleep modes. Eleven time-outs from 8 ms to 8 s. Normal mode has one time-out; Window mode adds a closed period. Settings are CCP-protected and can be locked.

A non-zero PERIOD in WDT.CTRLA enables the WDT; a non-zero WINDOW enables Window mode. WDT.CTRLA and the LOCK bit in WDT.STATUS are CCP-protected. The reset value of WDT.CTRLA comes from FUSE.WDTCFG, and when the fuse enables the WDT, LOCK is set at boot. The oscillator is not accurate, so the time-out varies from part to part and software has to allow for it.

Normal mode: each WDR starts a new time-out TOWDT, and a missed time-out resets the system. Window mode: a closed period TOWDTW (8 ms to 8 s) during which a WDR causes a reset is followed by an open period TOWDT (8 ms to 8 s) in which the WDR must come; the total time-out is their sum. The first closed period starts after the first WDR after enabling Window mode or leaving debug. A second WDR while one is synchronising is ignored.

Writing 1 to LOCK in WDT.STATUS freezes WDT.CTRLA so software cannot disable the watchdog. LOCK can only be set, and cleared only in debug mode; it is set automatically when the configuration comes from fuses.

The WDT runs in any sleep mode where its clock runs. A debug halt stops it and resets its counter; on restart in Window mode the first closed period is skipped and a normal time-out runs. Writes to PERIOD and WINDOW cross clock domains: SYNCBUSY in WDT.STATUS shows a synchronisation in progress, and WDT.CTRLA is not written while it is set. A WDR takes two to three WDT clock cycles to synchronise, and a WDR issued meanwhile is ignored.

A 16-bit timer/counter with three compare channels, double-buffered period and compare registers, frequency, single-slope and dual-slope PWM generation, counting on events, overflow interrupts and events, and one compare match per channel. It counts the prescaled peripheral clock or events, and events can also set its direction. In Split mode it becomes a pair of 8-bit timers, each having three compare channels.

CNT, PER, CMPn and the buffers PERBUF and CMPnBUF are 16-bit. CNT is compared continuously with zero, PER and each CMPn; an interrupt, event or output change follows on the next CLK_TCA cycle, CLK_TCA being the prescaled CLK_PER or an event. To start: write TOP to PER, set ENABLE in CTRLA; setting CNTEI in EVCTRL counts events instead of clock ticks. In normal operation the counter runs in the DIR direction of CTRLE: counting up it wraps to 0 after TOP, counting down it reloads PER at BOTTOM. A write to CNT takes effect at once and outranks count, clear and reload. Each buffer has a valid flag (PERBV, CMPnBV in CTRLF) set on a buffer write and cleared at UPDATE, when the buffer is copied in. Without buffering a new PER is used at once, and a PER below CNT makes the counter run to MAX and wrap before any compare match; with buffering PER changes only at UPDATE.

To put a waveform on a pin: choose a mode in WGMODE (CTRLB), set CMPnEN in CTRLB (this overrides the pin's OUT value; PORTMUX can pick an alternative pin), make the pin an output, and optionally invert it with INVEN in PINnCTRL. Frequency mode toggles the output on each compare match, with CMP0 setting the period. Single-slope PWM counts BOTTOM to TOP, sets the output at BOTTOM and clears it on match; CMPn = BOTTOM gives a constant low and CMPn > TOP a constant high. Dual-slope PWM counts up and down, clears on the up-count match and sets on the down-count match; CMPn = BOTTOM gives constant low and CMPn = TOP constant high, and its top frequency is half that of single-slope.

Software writes CMD in CTRLESET to issue UPDATE (as an UPDATE condition, but regardless of LUPD), RESTART (counter, direction and all compare outputs go to 0) or RESET (all registers to their reset values, allowed only while ENABLE = 0).

Split mode makes two 8-bit timers, LCNT and HCNT, each with three compare channels (outputs WOn from the low byte and WO[n+3] from the high byte). It counts down only, gives single-slope PWM only, takes no event inputs or event actions, leaves the buffer registers and valid flags unused, and gives byte access to all registers. The high byte has an underflow interrupt but no compare interrupts or flags. Register values carry across a change of mode while their meaning changes, so the peripheral should be disabled and hard-reset (CMD = RESET) before switching. To start: set SPLITM in CTRLD, write TOP to the PER registers, set ENABLE. All event generators except HUNF are shared by Normal and Split mode.

The event user acts as chosen by EVACT in EVCTRL once CNTEI is set. Each interrupt sets its flag in INTFLAGS, is enabled in INTCTRL, and its request stays active until the flag is cleared. TCA keeps running in Idle sleep mode.

A 16-bit timer/counter with eight modes: periodic interrupt; time-out check; four input capture modes (on event, frequency, pulse width, and both frequency and pulse width together); single-shot; and 8-bit PWM. It has a noise canceller on its event input and can run synchronised to TCA. It is clocked from CLK_PER, CLK_PER/2 or the clock of a TCA, chosen by CLKSEL in CTRLA; any event, such as an external clock on a pin, can drive its control logic through the event system.

TCB resets into Periodic Interrupt mode. Write TOP to CCMP, optionally set CCMPEN in CTRLB to put the waveform on its pin (overriding PORT), then set ENABLE in CTRLA. A CAPT interrupt and event follow when CNT reaches TOP; if CCMP is set below the present CNT, the counter runs to MAX and wraps. An event pulse must be longer than one system clock cycle to be sure of edge detection.

Periodic interrupt: counts to CCMP and restarts at BOTTOM, CAPT at TOP. Time-out check: starts on one event edge and stops on the next (EDGE in EVCTRL picks which); CAPT if CNT reaches TOP before the second edge. Input capture on event: counts BOTTOM to MAX continuously and copies CNT to CCMP on each selected edge; zero CNT when entering this mode. Frequency measurement: captures CNT and restarts on the selected edge. Pulse-width measurement: restarts on a rising edge and captures on the next falling edge, needing at least two clock cycles between edges. Frequency and pulse-width: starts on a rising edge, captures on the falling edge, stops on the next rising edge and sets the flag; read CNT before CCMP. In the capture modes the CAPT flag clears when the low byte of CCMP is read.

Single-shot gives one pulse of CCMP length per event edge: the output goes high and the counter runs BOTTOM to TOP, then the output goes low for at least one prescaler cycle, during which a new event is ignored. The output rises two clock cycles after the event, or at once with ASYNC = 1 in CTRLB, the counter still starting two to three CLK_TCB cycles later. RUN in STATUS shows whether it is counting. The counter starts as soon as the module is enabled, or with EDGE = 1, unless TOP is written to CNT first. In 8-bit PWM mode CCMPL sets the period (CCMPL+1 cycles) and CCMPH the high time; the output is set at BOTTOM and cleared when CNT reaches CCMPH.

Changing mode while enabled can give an unpredictable output, and a flag can be set during configuration, so INTFLAGS should be cleared after setting up. The noise canceller (FILTER in EVCTRL) passes the input only after four equal consecutive samples, adding four system clock cycles of delay; it runs on the system clock, not the prescaler. With CLKSEL set to the TCA clock the TCB counts on exactly the same clock as TCAn, and SYNCUPD = 1 restarts TCB whenever TCAn restarts.

With CAPTEI set in EVCTRL an event acts as set by EDGE and CNTMODE; it must last at least one CLK_PER cycle, except in asynchronous single-shot, where shorter edges are caught. TCB is halted in Standby unless RUNSTDBY in CTRLA is set, and halted in Power-Down.

A 12-bit waveform generator for control applications, with a counter that can run asynchronously to the peripheral clock, a programmable prescaler, double-buffered compare registers and four waveform modes: One Ramp, Two Ramp, Four Ramp and Dual Slope. Two compare/capture units drive outputs WOA and WOB with optional dead time; WOC and WOD can each copy WOA or WOB. Two event inputs give capture by event or software, a programmable input filter and conditional output control: fault handling, input blanking, overload protection and hardware emergency stop. It supports half-bridge and full-bridge outputs. The device has one instance, TCD0.

The TCD clock CLK_TCD is chosen by CLKSEL from four sources (OSCHF, PLL, EXTCLK, CLK_PER) and feeds three separate prescalers: the counter prescaler (CLK_TCD_CNT), the synchronizer prescaler (CLK_TCD_SYNC, its own clock so the TCD and I/O domains synchronise faster) and the delay prescaler (CLK_TCD_DLY, which times input blanking and the delayed event output). Counter and synchronizer prescalers are set in CTRLA, the delay prescaler in DLYCTRL. Each input event can use one of ten input modes.

To start: pick the clock and prescaler in CTRLA, the waveform mode in CTRLB, set the other static registers, write the CMPxSET/CLR values and other buffered registers, wait for ENRDY in STATUS, then set ENABLE. ENABLE can only be changed while ENRDY = 1. CTRLE is a self-clearing command strobe, synchronised once the TCD is enabled; CMDRDY in STATUS shows when a new command may be given. Double-buffered registers can be written while enabled when CMDRDY = 1, and reach the core on a synchronisation command or at enable. Static registers can be changed only while the TCD is disabled. Normal I/O and read-only registers have no synchronisation limits.

WGMODE in CTRLB picks the mode. A TCD cycle runs through four states in order (DTA and OTA, the dead and on time of WOA, then DTB and OTB for WOB), ended in turn by CMPASET, CMPACLR, CMPBSET and CMPBCLR. One Ramp counts up to CMPBCLR once per cycle; outputs do not overlap only if CMPASET < CMPACLR < CMPBSET < CMPBCLR; a CMPBCLR match clears all outputs, any compare value above CMPBCLR never acts, and CMPACLR below CMPASET has no effect. Two Ramp counts to CMPACLR, resets, then counts to CMPBCLR; the A and B values are independent and the outputs cannot overlap without override. Four Ramp resets after each of the four compare values, with no limits on their values and no overlap without override. Dual Slope counts down from CMPBCLR to zero and back up: WOA is set on the down-count match with CMPASET and cleared on the up-count match, WOB set on the up-count match with CMPBSET and cleared on the down-count match; outputs overlap if CMPASET > CMPBSET, and CMPACLR is unused. Dual Slope starts at CMPBCLR counting down, so WOB first sets on the up-count.
Writing ENABLE = 0 stops the TCD as soon as that reaches the core domain; writing DISEOC = 1 in CTRLE stops it at the end of the TCD cycle.

Inputs A and B come from the event system and act on WOA and WOB. TRIGEI in EVCTRLx enables an input; by default it is a fault input, and ACTION = 1 makes it a capture trigger as well; INPUTMODE = 0 in INPUTCTRLx turns fault detection off. Both inputs have the same ten modes, but only input A has input blanking. An event reaches the outputs after two to three synchronizer clock cycles, or at once with asynchronous detection (set by CFG in EVCTRLx), in which case the counter flow changes only once the event is synchronised. The digital filter (FILTER) removes pulses shorter than four counter clock cycles and delays every change by four; it cannot be combined with asynchronous detection.

Blanking ignores the inputs for a set time after a trigger chosen by DLYTRIG, enabled through DLYSEL in DLYCTRL, so that events caused by the outputs switching are masked. A counter on the delay clock (CLK_TCD_SYNC divided by DLYPRESC) runs up to DLYVAL and then blanking ends. It shares its logic with the programmable output event, so the two cannot be used together.

Mode 0: inputs do not touch the outputs but can still capture and interrupt. Mode 1: stop the output, go to the other output's dead time and hold there while the event is high; input A acts only in dead or on time A, input B only in dead or on time B. Mode 2: stop the output, run the opposite dead and on time, then wait if the event is still active. Mode 3: stop the output and repeat the opposite dead and on time while the fault lasts, then finish and resume. Mode 4 (either input): outputs off while the event lasts, counter unaffected. Mode 5: outputs off and alternating dead times while the event lasts. Mode 6: outputs off, move to the other output's dead time and hold while the event lasts. Mode 7: outputs and counter stop until a RESTART command, after which it starts on dead time A; it stops again if the event is still high. Mode 8: a rising edge during the matching on time ends it and jumps to the opposite dead time. Mode 9: a rising edge during the matching on time turns the output off for the rest of that on time, counter unaffected. Mode 10: the matching output stays off while the input is active and for the rest of an on time it is released in, counter unaffected.

When the prescaler and period cannot give the wanted frequency, the dither accumulates the fractional part of the period each cycle and adds one clock cycle when it overflows, to the part chosen by DITHERSEL in DITCTRL: the on time of B only or of both outputs, or the dead time of B only or of both. Where no cycle is added to the TCD cycle the following state is shortened instead; for example in One Ramp with dead time B selected, dead time B grows by one cycle and on time B shrinks by one. Dual Slope mode has no dithering. Example: a 10 MHz counter clock has 100 ns steps, and 75 kHz needs 133.33 cycles; 133 cycles gives 75.188 kHz and 134 gives 74.626 kHz, and dithering the 0.33-cycle remainder averages 75 kHz.

The asynchronous counter cannot be read directly; CAPTUREA and CAPTUREB capture it into the I/O domain, on input event A/B or by software. Read the low byte (CAPTUREAL/BL) first, then the high byte. With ACTION = 1 in EVCTRLx an input event captures and raises TRIGA/TRIGB in INTFLAGS (interrupt enabled in INTCTRL). Software capture: write SCAPTUREx in CTRLE, and the value is ready when CMDRDY in STATUS reads 1 again. One event can both capture and change the counter flow according to the input mode. Connecting both inputs to the same PWM event channel, one capturing rising and one falling edges, measures a PWM signal. In One Ramp, input B with INPUTMODE = 0x08 resets the counter on a capture.

FAULTCTRL configures the outputs: CMPxEN enables each output and CMPx sets its level on a fault. FAULTCTRL is cleared only by power-on reset and is loaded from FUSE.TCDCFG during every reset. CMPCSEL and CMPDSEL in CTRLC route WOC and WOD to WOA or WOB. CMPOVR in CTRLC enables override, with CMPAVAL and CMPBVAL in CTRLD giving the output values in each dead and on time; in One Ramp, WOA uses only the DTA/OTA settings and WOB only DTB/OTB. With override and fault input modes together, the CMPA bit in FAULTCTRL (and CMPC/D when they follow WOA) must equal CMPAVAL[0] and [2], and likewise CMPB with CMPBVAL[0] and [2], or the first cycle after a fault can have the wrong polarity. In any input mode other than 0, an input event can cause nanosecond spikes on an unloaded output, always towards the FAULTCTRL CMPx level.

The three compare-match events last one counter clock cycle; the programmable event PROGEV lasts one synchronizer clock cycle. PROGEV shares trigger and delay logic with input blanking, so with blanking in use it cannot be delayed and uses the blanking trigger. It is set in DLYCTRL and DLYVAL and can be delayed by 0 to 255 delay clock cycles: TCD clock period × DLYPRESC factor × DLYVAL.

TRIGA and TRIGB share the TRIG vector; INTFLAGS tells them apart. TCD runs in Idle and stops in Standby and Power-Down. A debug halt stops it unless DBGRUN in DBGCTRL is set; with FAULTDET set, a halt raises a fault on both inputs for as long as the break lasts, which can switch external parts off. FAULTCTRL is under configuration change protection (IOREG key): the key is written to CPU.CCP and the protected write must follow within four instructions, otherwise the register is unchanged.

The RTC peripheral holds two timers on one clock, CLK_RTC: the real-time counter and the periodic interrupt timer, each enabled separately. The RTC is a 16-bit counter behind a 15-bit prescaler, with one period and one compare register; it raises the compare interrupt/event on the first count after CNT equals CMP, and the overflow interrupt/event on the first count after CNT equals PER, which also clears CNT. CLK_RTC is a 32.768 kHz crystal, an external clock, the 32.768 kHz OSCULP32K, or OSCULP32K divided by 32. At 32.768 kHz the finest step is 30.5 µs with time-outs up to two seconds; with 1 s steps the longest time-out is 65536 s, over 18 hours. The PIT raises an interrupt every n CLK_RTC cycles, n from 4 to 32768 in powers of two, or a level event with n from 64 to 8192. The RTC can run in sleep and wake the device.

CLK_PER must be at least four times CLK_RTC to read the counter, whatever the prescaler. A 32.768 kHz crystal with its load capacitors connects to TOSC1 and TOSC2; an external digital clock goes to TOSC1. Set up the oscillator in CLKCTRL first, then choose it with CLKSEL in RTC.CLKSEL; RTC and PIT share this choice.

RTC: write CMP and/or PER, enable the CMP and OVF interrupts in INTCTRL, set PRESCALER in CTRLA, then set RTCEN; clearing RTCEN disables it. PIT: configure CLK_RTC, set PI in PITINTCTRL, choose PERIOD in PITCTRLA, then set PITEN. The RTC is used internally during start-up, so the busy flags in STATUS and PITSTATUS must be checked, including at first configuration.

The RTC and PIT share the prescaler's counter, which runs whenever either is enabled. So the earliest PIT interrupt and RTC tick come anywhere from immediately to one full period after enabling. After the first interrupt the PIT output toggles every half period; for PERIOD = CYC16 it follows prescaler bit 3, giving one interrupt every 16 CLK_RTC cycles.

operation.topic: RTC interrupts, sleep, synchronisation and debug
operation.text: The RTC has two flag registers (INTFLAGS, PITINTFLAGS) and two enable registers (INTCTRL, PITINTCTRL). The RTC runs in Idle, and in Standby when RUNSTDBY in CTRLA is set; the PIT runs in every sleep mode. Both run from CLK_RTC, so control and count writes take some cycles to take effect; busy flags CMPBUSY, PERBUSY, CNTBUSY and CTRLABUSY in STATUS and CTRLBUSY in PITSTATUS must be checked before writing those registers. In a debug halt the RTC stops and ignores events unless DBGRUN in DBGCTRL is set; the PIT output goes low unless DBGRUN in PITDBGCTRL is set, and if it was high at the break an extra PIT interrupt occurs on restart.

A serial port for full duplex, or half duplex in one-wire or RS-485 form, asynchronous or synchronous, with frames of 5 to 9 data bits and 1 or 2 stop bits. A fractional baud generator makes the baud rate from any system clock without a crystal. It checks odd or even parity, detects buffer overflow and frame errors, filters noise (false start bit detection, digital low-pass), and has separate transmit complete, data register empty and receive complete interrupts. It can also act as an SPI master, does multiprocessor communication, start-of-frame detection, IrDA pulse coding (IRCOM) and LIN slave. The transmitter has a one-entry buffer and a shift register; the receiver a two-level buffer and a shift register.

Full duplex: set BAUD, set frame format and mode in CTRLC, make TXD an output, enable transmitter and receiver in CTRLB. One-wire half duplex: set LBME in CTRLA to join TXD to the receiver, enable the pin pull-up (PULLUPEN), set ODME in CTRLB for open drain (TXD then becomes an output automatically), set BAUD and CTRLC, and enable transmitter and receiver. Global interrupts should be off while setting up an interrupt-driven USART, and no transfer should be in progress when baud rate or frame format is changed.

A frame is a low start bit, 5 to 9 data bits, an optional even or odd parity bit and 1 or 2 high stop bits; the idle line is high. The shift clock comes from the fractional baud generator or from XCK. BAUD holds the division factor shifted left six bits, the low six bits being the fraction that trims the rate; the integer part must be at least 1, so BAUD runs 64 to 65535. In synchronous mode only BAUD[15:6] counts and BAUD[5:0] must be zero.

Writing TXDATA (allowed when DREIF is set) starts a frame once the shift register is free; TXCIF sets when the frame is out and nothing waits in the buffer. For 9-bit characters write TXDATAH before TXDATAL; fewer than 8 bits ignore the unused high bits. Disabling the transmitter waits for pending data, then hands TXD back to PORT as an input. The receiver pin must be an input; a valid start bit starts sampling, only the first stop bit is checked, and the frame goes to the buffer and sets RXCIF. For 9-bit characters read RXDATAH first (for 9BITL, RXDATAL first). The error flags FERR, BUFOVF and PERR travel with each frame in RXDATAH, which must be read before the byte that shifts the buffer. Disabling the receiver is immediate and flushes the buffer; reading the data registers until RXCIF clears also flushes it.

In synchronous mode one master supplies XCK: the pin is an output for master, input for slave. Data are sampled on the XCK edge opposite the one they are sent on; with INVEN = 0 a bit starts on the rising edge and is sampled on the falling edge, INVEN = 1 swaps the edges. As slave, BAUD has no effect and XCK must stay below fCLK_PER/4.

Master SPI mode always sends 8 data bits with no start, stop or parity, LSb or MSb first by UDORD in CTRLC. The fractional baud generator makes the clock; INVEN and UCPHA choose the edges. Transmit and receive flags and interrupts are as in normal operation, except that the receive error flags read 0. It matches a stand-alone SPI in frame and timing but lacks write collision protection, double speed and multi-master support, and has no slave select pin.

The receiver samples 16 times per bit in normal mode and 8 times in double-speed mode (RXMODE = 0x01 in CTRLB). A falling edge from idle starts start-bit detection; samples 8, 9 and 10 (4, 5 and 6 at double speed) decide, and two or three lows accept the start bit. Every data and parity bit is decided by majority of its three centre samples. Only the first stop bit is checked; a low stop bit sets the frame error flag. A new start bit may begin right after the voting samples of the stop bit in normal mode, one sample later in double-speed mode. Normal mode tolerates more baud rate error than double-speed.

Double speed (RXMODE = 0x01) doubles the baud rate for a given setting and halves the samples per bit to 8, so it needs a more accurate clock and baud setting. Auto-baud sets BAUD from a break field followed by a sync field: a break is 12 or more low samples, then a counter at the peripheral clock times the next 8 bit times of the sync field and its result becomes BAUD. Generic mode (GENAUTO) can accept a break of any length when WFB in STATUS is set, and updates BAUD only for a result of 0x0064 to 0xFFFF. LIN mode (LINAUTO) needs a break of at least 12 peripheral clock cycles and a sync character of 0x55; any other sets ISFIF in STATUS and leaves the baud rate unchanged.

One-wire mode (LBME in CTRLA) joins TXD to the receiver, making TXD a shared TxD/RxD line and freeing RXD for other use. Open-drain mode (ODME in CTRLB) stops the transmitter from driving high, so with the pin pull-up any device can pull the line low without a short; the USART also receives its own transmission, which can reveal collisions. RS-485 mode is set in the RS485 field of CTRLA: RS485[0] drives XDIR high from one baud clock before the frame until the end of its stop bits, to enable an external line driver; RS485[1] makes TXD an output one clock cycle before transmission and an input again afterwards. RS-485 can be combined with one-wire mode.

With CMODE = 0x02 in CTRLC the USART encodes and decodes IrDA 1.4 pulses up to 115.2 kbps; TXD/RXD carry the inverted pulse. The receiver can take its input from an event channel instead of RXD. Transmit pulses are 3/16 of the bit period, a fixed programmable width based on the peripheral clock, or off. Received pulses shorter than a programmable minimum are discarded and read as 1. Double speed cannot be used with IRCOM.

operation.topic: USART parity, start-of-frame and multiprocessor mode
operation.text: PMODE in CTRLC chooses even or odd parity; a mismatch sets PERR in RXDATAH. In LIN auto-baud mode (RXMODE = 0x03) parity is checked only on the protected identifier field. Start-of-frame detection (SFDEN in CTRLB, asynchronous only) wakes the device from Standby on a falling edge on RXD: the oscillator starts and the frame can be received if the baud rate is slow enough for the oscillator start-up time; RXSIF is set, sharing the RXC interrupt line with RXCIF, and a false start bit returns the device to Standby. Multiprocessor mode (MPCM in CTRLB) marks address frames with a 1 in the first stop bit (5 to 8 data bits, transmitter using two stop bits) or the ninth bit; unaddressed slaves ignore data frames until the next address, and the addressed slave clears MPCM to receive data and sets it again afterwards.
Each interrupt sets its flag in STATUS and is enabled in CTRLA; the request stays active until the flag is cleared.

A synchronous serial interface on three or four pins, full duplex, master or slave, LSb or MSb first, with seven bit rates, an end-of-transfer interrupt flag, write collision protection, wake from Idle and a double-speed (CK/2) master mode. The master pulls the chosen slave's SS low and clocks SCK; data move master to slave on MOSI and slave to master on MISO through an 8-bit shift register in each device. A write to DATA lands in the shift register (Normal mode) or the transmit buffer (Buffer mode); a read returns the receive register or the receive buffer in the same way. A slave synchronises and samples the incoming SCK.

Configure the SS pin, choose master or slave with MASTER in CTRLA, in master mode set PRESC and CLK2X in CTRLA, then optionally MODE in CTRLB, DORD in CTRLA, BUFEN and BUFWR in CTRLB and SSD in CTRLB (to disable multi-master), and finally set ENABLE in CTRLA.

Writing DATA starts a transfer. Normal mode is single-buffered for transmit and double-buffered for receive: DATA must not be written before the transfer ends (a write corrupts the data and sets WRCOL), and the received byte must be read before the next transfer completes; IF in INTFLAGS sets after each transfer. Buffer mode (BUFEN = 1; BUFWR has no effect for a master) is double-buffered for transmit and triple-buffered for receive: DATA may be written while DREIF is set, received bytes enter a two-entry FIFO that must be emptied no less often than every other transfer, and TXCIF sets when shift register and transmit buffer are both empty. With SSD = 0 and SS an input, SS must stay high; a low SS means another master is taking the bus, so MASTER is cleared, the SPI becomes a slave and IF is set; software must check MASTER before each write when SS may go low, and set it again to return to master. With SSD = 0 and SS an output, or with SSD = 1, the SS pin is free for other use.

SCK low and high times must each exceed two peripheral clock cycles. In Normal mode the slave idles while SS is high and shifts out from the first SCK edge after SS goes low; IF sets after each byte, and a write to DATA during a transfer is ignored and sets WRCOL. SS going high halts the logic and discards a partial byte. Buffer mode adds flags and buffers: with BUFWR = 0 the first byte sent is a dummy (whatever was in the shift register), as all writes go to the transmit buffer; with BUFWR = 1 the first written byte goes straight to the shift register while SS is high and is sent first. In both, a write while DREIF is low is lost; DREIF drops on each buffer write and rises when the buffer moves to the shift register; RXCIF follows one cycle after DREIF rises, and TXCIF one cycle after RXCIF once shift register and buffer are both sent. As a slave, the SS, SCK and MOSI pins are inputs at all times.

operation.topic: SPI data modes, events and interrupts
operation.text: MODE in CTRLB picks one of four combinations of SCK phase and polarity; data are shifted out and sampled on opposite edges. Within a clock cycle the leading edge comes first and the trailing edge last. The master SCK is available as an event. Each interrupt sets its flag in INTFLAGS, is enabled in INTCTRL, and stays active until its flag is cleared.

An I2C-compatible two-wire interface (standard, fast and fast mode plus) that is also SMBus 2.0 compatible: arbitration between start/repeated start and data bits, slave arbitration for the address resolution protocol, and SMBus layer 1 time-outs in hardware. Master and slave work independently on the same pins, single or multi-master with full arbitration. Slave address match works in all sleep modes, with 7-bit and general call recognition and either an address mask or a second address. It has an input filter against bus noise, Smart mode and Quick Command mode. The master's baud generator covers 100 kHz to 1 MHz. Start and stop conditions, collisions, bus errors, lost arbitration and clock hold are flagged in both master and slave. SDA and SCL are open-collector (wired-AND) lines.

The master issues a Start, sends a 7-bit address and a read/write bit, and the addressed slave acknowledges; each data packet is eight bits plus an acknowledge bit from the receiver; the master ends with a Stop. Only masters control the bus, and arbitration decides between masters.

SDASETUP, SDAHOLD and FMPEN in CTRLA must be set before the TWI is enabled. Master: write MBAUD for a valid bus clock, set ENABLE in MCTRLA, and write 0x1 to BUSSTATE in MSTATUS to force the bus to Idle. Slave: write the address to SADDR and set ENABLE in SCTRLA; the slave then waits for a Start and its address.

The master works byte by byte with optional interrupts, separate read and write flags, and status flags for ACK/NACK, bus error, lost arbitration, clock hold and bus state. A set interrupt flag holds SCL low until it is cleared. Standard mode runs to 100 kHz, fast mode to 400 kHz and fast mode plus to 1 MHz; MBAUD must give a frequency at or below the mode's limit. The bus state logic runs whenever the master is enabled, in all sleep modes including Power-Down. Writing MADDR (address and direction) starts a transaction, waiting for Idle if the bus is Busy. After the address: M1, write acknowledged, WIF set with RXACK = 0 and CLKHOLD = 1; M2, read acknowledged, the slave sends straight away; M3, no acknowledge, WIF and RXACK set, and a Stop by MCMD in MCTRLB is the recommended next step; M4, arbitration lost (WIF and ARBLOST) or bus error (BUSERR as well), the bus goes Busy and the master must wait for Idle. Writing MDATA sends a byte and clears WIF; RXACK is valid only with WIF set and ARBLOST and BUSERR clear. On reading, RIF and CLKHOLD set after each byte, and the ACKACT bit in MCTRLB is sent when the next command is written to MCMD. RIF and WIF are never set together.

BUSSTATE in MSTATUS reports the bus as Unknown (0b00), Idle (0b01), Owner (0b10) or Busy (0b11), worked out from start and stop detection, collision detection, inactive-bus time-out and a bit counter. It is Unknown after the master is enabled, after a system reset and after the master is disabled. Software can force only Idle, by writing 0x1; otherwise the bus becomes Idle at the first Stop, or on a time-out when TIMEOUT in MCTRLA is non-zero. An external Start on an idle bus makes it Busy until a Stop or time-out. A Start issued by this master makes it Owner; it returns to Idle after the master's Stop, or goes Busy until a Stop if arbitration is lost.

The slave works byte by byte with separate data and address/stop flags, and status for ACK/NACK, clock hold, collision, bus error and direction; a set flag holds SCL low. APIF in SSTATUS sets on a match with ADDR[7:1] in SADDR, on the general call address 0x00 when ADDR[0] is set, on the second address or mask in SADDRMASK when ADDREN is set, or on any address when PMEN in SCTRLA is set. Cases: S1, address accepted for a write; S2, accepted for a read, with DIF set; S3, a Stop received, with AP = 0; S4, collision, when the slave cannot send a high bit or NACK: COLL is set, its outputs are disabled and the clock released. COLL is meant for ARP systems; elsewhere a collision is a protocol violation to treat as a bus error. Received data set DIF and the ACKACT bit in SCTRLB is sent when SCMD is written; after sending, RXACK in SSTATUS shows the master's ACK or NACK.

operation.topic: TWI SMBus, multi-master, Smart mode, Quick Command, 10-bit address
operation.text: For SMBus, set TIMEOUT in MCTRLA, after MBAUD since the time-out depends on it; 100 kHz can be used. Standard and fast mode outputs are slew-rate limited; fast mode plus has ten times the output drive. SDAHOLD gives an SMBus-compatible SDA hold time. A master may start only on an idle bus; a master that fails to send a high bit loses arbitration, sees Busy and waits for Idle. Smart mode (SMEN in MCTRLA or SCTRLA) sends ACK automatically when MDATA or SDATA is read (master only when ACKACT is ACK), and on the slave clears DIF when SDATA is read or written. Quick Command (QCEN in MCTRLA) carries the command in the R/W bit with no data; after the ACK, RIF or WIF sets and a Stop may be issued. For a 10-bit address the master always starts with R/W = 0; the slave hardware recognises only the first byte, when the top five bits of SADDR are 0b11110, and software handles the second byte as data.

Several conditions share each vector, so the flags in MSTATUS or SSTATUS show which is present. Bus state logic and address recognition work in every sleep mode; a slave woken by its address stretches the clock until the main clock runs. The master stops in all sleep modes. The TWI halts with the CPU in debug unless DBGRUN in DBGCTRL is set; then MDATA and SDATA accesses neither start bus operations nor change flags.

A CRC-16-CCITT check of the whole Flash, the boot section, or boot and application sections, with an optional non-maskable interrupt on failure and an optional check during reset. The last location of the checked section must hold the pre-computed 16-bit checksum; a match sets the OK status, a mismatch shows as failure in STATUS. An n-bit CRC catches any error burst up to n bits and a fraction 1-2^-n of longer ones.

Write SRC in CTRLB, then set ENABLE in CTRLA; the scan starts three cycles later while the CPU keeps running. CRCSRC in FUSE.SYSCFG0 can make the scan run before the device leaves reset: on success code starts, ENABLE = 1, SRC shows the sections and OK = 1; on failure the CPU hangs without running code, with OK = 0, visible through the debugger. In Priority mode the CRC has priority access to Flash and stalls the CPU until done, fetching a 16-bit word every third main clock cycle, as it also does in the start-up scan. The checksum high byte sits two bytes before the section end and the low byte at the last byte.

A failure clears OK in STATUS. NMIEN in CTRLA enables the NMI, which only a system reset can disable; the NMI stays active until reset and fires even with interrupts globally disabled. CRCSCAN halts in every sleep mode and resumes when the CPU wakes.

Sleep can be entered during the three cycles before a scan starts; the scan then waits for the CPU to wake, and any interrupt handler runs after the scan. Any debugger access to a peripheral or memory disables CRCSCAN; a scan in progress restarts when the debugger touches an internal register or disconnects, and BUSY reads 1 meanwhile. The debugger can read synchronised CRC status without disabling it. From the debugger, writing BUSY = 0 stops a scan, BUSY = 1 starts one check with the CTRLB settings once allowed; while BUSY = 1, CTRLB and NMIEN cannot change. Writing OK = 0 can raise the NMI if NMIEN = 1, after which CRCSCAN takes no writes; OK = 1 makes OK read 1 while BUSY = 0. Debugger writes to CTRLA and CTRLB act as CPU writes.

Programmable glue logic with two look-up tables, LUT0 and LUT1. Each LUT takes three inputs, which can be masked, through a truth table to any logic function of up to three inputs, followed by an optional synchroniser, filter or edge detector. A sequential block driven by the LUT pair can act as a D flip-flop with gate, a JK flip-flop, a D latch with gate, or an RS latch. Inputs can come from pins, events, the other LUT, the analog comparators, timer/counter waveform outputs, the USART and the SPI. The CCL is clocked by the system clock or another peripheral, and its outputs go to pins or the event system. It needs CLKCTRL, PORT, EVSYS and UPDI set up, and has no interrupts.

The CCL runs on CLK_PER by default; CLKSRC = 1 in LUTnCTRLA clocks a LUT and its sequential block from its input IN[2] instead, the sequential block sharing the clock of the even LUT of the pair. With CLKSRC = 1 the truth table sees IN[2] as a masked, low input. The CCL must be disabled (ENABLE = 0 in CTRLA) while the clock source is changed. SEQSEL in SEQCTRL0 can be written only while the even LUT is disabled, and LUTnCTRLx (except ENABLE) only while that LUT is disabled; protected bits may be written together with setting ENABLE but not with clearing it. CTRLA ENABLE turns the CCL on and off; each LUT has its own ENABLE in LUTnCTRLA. Pins used must be configured for the LUT. The CCL keeps running and cannot be halted while the CPU is halted in debug.

INSEL0 and INSEL1 in LUTnCTRLB and INSEL2 in LUTnCTRLC choose each input: masked, FEEDBACK (the pair's sequential output), LINK (the next LUT's direct output: LUT1 feeds LUT0, and LUT0 feeds the last LUT), EVENT0 or EVENT1 (asynchronous events, the event system set up first), the LUT's own I/O pin, or a peripheral.

operation.topic: CCL filter, edge detector and sequential logic
operation.text: FILTSEL in LUTnCTRLA adds a synchroniser or filter that removes glitches and delays the output by two to five clock cycles; filter state clears one clock after the LUT is disabled. EDGEDET = 1 makes a pulse on each rising edge (an inverted truth table gives falling edges) and needs a filter option enabled to behave predictably. SEQSEL in SEQCTRLn picks the sequential function; the even LUT drives D, J or S and the odd LUT drives G, K or R. Disabling the even LUT clears the latch asynchronously, holding the flip-flop reset for one clock cycle.

Each LUT output LUTnOUT is an event; incoming events can be LUT inputs. With RUNSTDBY = 1 in CTRLA the system clock stays on in Standby; otherwise it stops, and a LUT using filter, edge detector or sequential logic outputs 0 in Standby. In Idle the truth table keeps working whatever RUNSTDBY says. A LUT clocked from IN[2] depends on that source still running in sleep. The CCL has no configuration change protection.

Each comparator compares one positive and one negative input and outputs 1 when the positive input is higher, 0 otherwise. Response time is 50 ns above 2.7 V supply. It offers zero-cross detection, hysteresis of none, 10, 25 or 50 mV, output to a pin, output inversion, interrupts on rising, falling or both edges, and its output as an event. Positive inputs are up to four pins; negative inputs are up to two pins, the DAC output or the internal reference.

AINNn and AINPn are analog inputs, configured in PORT and PORTMUX; disabling the GPIO input buffer on them is recommended. The AC runs on the peripheral clock. To start: set up the pins, choose inputs with MUXPOS and MUXNEG in MUXCTRLA, optionally set OUTEN in CTRLA for the pin output, then set ENABLE. The output may be invalid during start-up: at most 2.5 µs for the AC itself, and up to 60 µs for VREF when an internal reference is used. Debug mode does not affect it.

operation.topic: AC inputs, hysteresis and low power
operation.text: HYSMODE in CTRLA sets off or one of three hysteresis levels. Pin inputs are AINN0, AINN1, AINP0, AINP1, AINP2 and AINP3, though low pin-count packages lack some. Internal inputs are the DAC output and the AC voltage reference. LPMODE in CTRLA lowers power at the cost of longer propagation delay.

The comparator output is an event source whenever the AC is enabled, asynchronous to all clocks; the AC has no event inputs. The interrupt flag is in STATUS and is enabled in INTCTRL. The AC runs in Idle. In Standby it is off unless RUNSTDBY in CTRLA is set; then it runs, and events and the pin output update, but STATUS is not updated and no interrupts occur unless another module keeps CLK_PER running. In Power-Down the AC and its pin output are off. No configuration change protection.

A 10-bit converter for 0 V to VDD inputs, single-ended against GND, through an analog multiplexer from pins or internal sources. It has internal references, an external reference input (VREFA) and VDD as reference, free-running or single conversions, a conversion-complete interrupt and an optional interrupt on the result (window comparator: under, over, inside or outside thresholds), a temperature sensor channel, event-triggered conversion, and accumulation of up to 64 samples per result. A sample delay, optionally varied automatically, moves the sampling frequency within a burst away from harmonic noise. A sample-and-hold keeps the input constant during conversion. When the PTC is enabled it takes full control of ADC0.

MUXPOS chooses any ADC pin, GND, the internal reference or the temperature sensor. Reference and channel choices take effect only once ENABLE in CTRLA is set; with ENABLE = 0 the ADC draws no power. The result in RES is right-adjusted.

Set RESSEL in CTRLA, optionally FREERUN in CTRLA and SAMPNUM in CTRLB, choose REFSEL in CTRLC (default: the internal VREF), set PRESC in CTRLC for CLK_ADC, choose MUXPOS, optionally set STARTEI in EVCTRL with the event system set up, then set ENABLE. Conversions start by event or by writing STCONV in COMMAND. The digital input buffer of an ADC pin should be disabled in PORT for best results.

STCONV stays 1 while a conversion runs and clears when a single conversion ends. A channel change during a conversion waits for it to finish. RESRDY in INTFLAGS sets at the end, whether or not its interrupt is enabled, so it can be polled. With STARTEI set, any event routed to the ADC starts a conversion on its edge by setting STCONV. In free-running mode the first STCONV starts a chain of back-to-back conversions.

For full 10-bit resolution CLK_ADC must be 50 kHz to 1.5 MHz; at lower resolution it may be faster for a higher sample rate. The prescaler divides CLK_PER (above 100 kHz) by 2 to 256 and runs while ENABLE = 1, but is held reset between conversions, giving a fixed start delay after each trigger; a conversion starts on the next CLK_ADC rising edge. A conversion takes 13 CLK_ADC cycles, with sample-and-hold two cycles after the start. RESRDY clears when RES is read or when 1 is written to it. SAMPDLY (CTRLD) and SAMPLEN (SAMPCTRL) lengthen sampling for high-impedance sources without slowing the clock; INITDLY delays the first conversion by 0 to 256 CLK_ADC cycles.

MUXPOS and REFSEL pass through a buffer and follow writes until a conversion starts, are then locked, and follow again from the last CLK_ADC cycle before RESRDY. In single mode select the channel before starting; it may change one ADC clock cycle after STCONV is written. In free-running mode the result after a change still reflects the old channel, the one after that the new channel. Switching channels needs a settling time. Inputs above VREF read as full scale, 0x3FF. REFSEL picks VDD (through a passive switch), VREFA or the internal VREF; with VREFA, ADCnREFSEL in VREF.CTRLn is set to the nearest level above the applied voltage, and 0x3 for references above 4.3 V. The internal reference comes from a bandgap through an amplifier in VREF.

Each ADC pin carries its pin capacitance and leakage whether selected or not; when selected the source charges the sample-and-hold capacitor through the input path resistance. Sources of about 10 kΩ or less give negligible sampling time; higher impedances need longer, by an amount that varies widely.

Set VREF to 1.1 V and REFSEL to 0x0, select the temperature sensor channel in MUXPOS (this turns the sensor on), set INITDLY ≥ 32 µs × fCLK_ADC in CTRLD and SAMPLEN ≥ 32 µs × fCLK_ADC in SAMPCTRL, set SAMPCAP = 1 in CTRLC, and convert. The output is linear in temperature but varies between devices; production test stores a gain correction in SIGROW.TEMPSENSE0 and an offset correction in SIGROW.TEMPSENSE1, applied in software.

WINLT and WINHT set the thresholds and WINCM in CTRLE the condition (under, over, inside, outside); a non-zero WINCM enables it, and WCMP in INTCTRL enables the interrupt. With accumulation the comparison is made once, after the last sample.

A result ready event, one clock period long, is generated whenever the ADC is enabled. In Standby the ADC stops unless RUNSTDBY in CTRLA is set; then conversions in progress finish and interrupts run, and new conversions must come from events or free-running mode started before sleep, the peripheral clock being requested as needed. A non-zero INITDLY gives the reference and supply time to settle in Standby. In Power-Down no conversion is possible; one in progress halts and resumes on wake, and its result is invalid even though RESRDY sets.

An 8-bit resistor-string DAC converting up to 350 ksps between GND and the reference chosen in VREF. DAC0 has a continuous-time output driver able to drive 5 kΩ and/or 30 pF on pin PA6; the other DACs feed only internal peripherals. Each DAC is wired internally to the AC and ADC. It runs on the peripheral clock, has no interrupts or events, and is unaffected by debug mode.

Choose the reference with DACnREFSEL in VREF.CTRLx, route the output to the AC or ADC and/or set OUTEN in CTRLA for the pin (DAC0 only, PORT configured), write an initial DATA value, then set ENABLE in CTRLA. While enabled, each write to DATA starts a conversion; while disabled, setting ENABLE starts it. For internal use only, OUTEN may stay 0.

With RUNSTDBY in CTRLA set and CLK_PER available, the DAC runs in Standby; otherwise the DAC and output buffer are switched off in Standby and come back on waking, needing a start-up time before a new conversion. In Power-Down they are off. No configuration change protection.

The PTC measures capacitive touch sensors drawn as PCB electrodes and wired to its pins, in mutual-capacitance mode (X-Y matrices, including ITO grids, one pin per X line and one per Y line) or self-capacitance mode (one Y pin per sensor), mixed as needed. It suits low-power buttons, sliders and wheels, wakes the device on touch from Standby, needs one pin per electrode and no external parts, compensates parasitic capacitance with adjustable gain, auto-calibrates against temperature and VDD drift, measures single-shot or free-running, filters noise in hardware and desynchronises against conducted noise, and can drive any X/Y line as a shield with all enabled sensors at the scanned sensor's potential. Channel change delay is selectable, acquisition starts by command or auto-trigger, and an acquisition-complete interrupt keeps CPU load low. The available pins depend on package and configuration.

The Y lines pass through a series resistor RS into a charge integrator with compensation, converted by the 10-bit ADC; X lines are driven digitally. External components are not needed, but a series resistor of 1 kΩ or more on X and Y lines improves EMC. A mutual-capacitance sensor is an X (transmit) and a Y (sense) electrode whose mutual capacitance is measured; a self-capacitance sensor is one Y electrode whose capacitance is measured. The PTC runs on CLK_PER and uses the ADC, which must be enabled and configured. It is driven through the QTouch Library, configured with the Atmel START QTouch Configurator and linked with the application.

operation.topic: UPDI, unified program and debug interface
operation.text: A one-wire interface on the RESET pin through which an outside tool programs the part and debugs it on chip. It talks an asynchronous half-duplex UART protocol to the programmer and takes no GPIO pin. It writes the Flash, the EEPROM, the fuses, the lock bits and the user row, and gives a debugger memory-mapped access to NVM, RAM and I/O whatever the device clock, with unlimited software breakpoints and two hardware breakpoints, run-time readout of PC, SP and SREG, break/stop detection and run, stop and reset control. It has built-in error detection with error signatures, can skip response generation for faster programming, and on a locked device still reads out the result of the Flash CRC check. Some registers are reachable only after the right key has been sent and only in OCD Stopped or certain programming modes.

Three protocol layers: the physical layer (PHY) runs the UART on the pin with clock and data recovery; the data link layer (DL) decodes instructions; the access layer (ACC) reaches the bus matrix, through which it gets to memory, NVM and every peripheral. The ASI (asynchronous system interface) is a second path for the debugger, to selected OCD, NVM and system-management features, that needs no bus request.

The PHY layer runs from a dedicated internal oscillator (CLK_UPDI); the ACC layer runs on the peripheral clock (CLK_PER), with a synchroniser between them. CLK_UPDI starts at 4 MHz after the UPDI is enabled or reset and is changed with UPDICLKDIV in UPDI.ASI_CTRLA.

The PHY supports one-wire asynchronous mode (half-duplex UART on the UPDI pin), detects the baud rate and recovers clock and data from each frame, detects parity, clock-recovery, frame and system errors, generates ACK responses and error signatures, and controls guard time. The RESET pin becomes the UPDI pin through RSTPINCFG in FUSE.SYSCFG0 or through the high-voltage enable sequence, not through the PORT settings; while the UPDI is active it controls the pin's pull-up, input and output enables itself.

The programmer always starts a transfer with a SYNCH character; the UPDI measures it and uses that rate for receiving and sending the following instruction and data. There is no baud rate register to write. Receive and transmit rates are equal within the auto-baud accuracy, and the usable range follows the UPDI clock set by UPDICLKDIV. The baud generator counts fractionally to keep the error small.

A BREAK resets the UPDI's internal state, for example after an error or lost synchronisation, and sets the UPDI clock back to the 4 MHz default. The debugger sends two BREAKs in a row: one sent while the UPDI is busy receiving or transmitting is missed but aborts the operation with a frame or contention error, and the second is then seen. At the slowest UPDI clock (4 MHz, 250 ns) the longest SYNCH the UPDI can hold in 16 bits is 2.05 ms per bit, so a BREAK of 12 such bits lasts about 24.6 ms; with a known prescaler setting it can be shorter.

SYNCH is 0x55 in the normal frame. It enables the UPDI after it has been disabled, and the baud generator measures it (each bit toggles) to set the rate for the next transfer; a bad SYNCH means the next transfer is sampled wrongly. One goes before each instruction; after REPEAT only the first instruction needs one. The SYNCH of the enable sequence also serves the first instruction.

The UPDI pin has a permanent pull-up. The programmer starts up the UPDI by pulling the pin low for more than 200 ns; an edge detector then holds the pin low itself while the UPDI oscillator starts, and lets go once it runs. The programmer polls the pin after its own release and, once it reads high, sends a SYNCH; when that is received the UPDI is enabled and waits for the first instruction. The typical hold time is 256 cycles of a 32 MHz oscillator plus calibration readout; the UPDI timing table gives the limits. If the edge detector fires by accident, the UPDI does not stay on: it turns itself off again.

With RSTPINCFG in FUSE.SYSCFG0 at 0x1 the UPDI owns the RESET pin as an input with pull-up.
